newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech cenbank rejects monetary policy critics - CTK.
newsitem.headline: Czech cenbank rejects monetary policy critics - CTK.

text.p: Czech National Bank (CNB) governor Josef Tosovsky rejected government criticism of the CNB's restrictive monetary policy, saying it was not sacrificing economic growth, CTK news agency said on Wednesday.
Tosovsky was also quoted by CTK as saying he was sticking to his original 1997 average inflation prediction of eight percent.
Tosovsky was reported to have told the parliamentary budget committee the economy's main problem was the current account deficit, which reached 8.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) last year.
He said a current account deficit of between four and five percent of GDP was considered the internationally acceptable maximum.
"It (8.6 percent) is already a spectre for investors," CTK quoted the governor as saying.
Tosovsky said monetary policy was not as tight as it looked because overall credit had been steadily increasing and bank interest rates were on a generally downward trend, CTK said.
He also rejected an idea that the money supply decline was connected with the drop in output.
While overall M2 money growth fell to 7.1 percent in January after 17.8 in the same month last year, economic growth has also fallen to 4.4 percent in 1996 from 4.8 percent the year before.
The government last week halved its 1997 economic growth estimate to a maximum of 2.7 percent.

The foreign exchange market has been nervous in recent days, with many dealers fearing the CNB will heed government calls for a relaxation of monetary policy, including a rate cut, in the wake of government fiscal restricitons announced last week as part of an economic revival package.

The package cut government spending and imposed import restrictions to rein in budget and foreign trade deficits. In return for fiscal tightening, the government called for a slackening of monetary policy.

The CNB raised the discount rate to 10.5 percent from 9.5 percent last June, raised the Lombard rate to 14.0 percent from 12.5 percent, and raised the minimum reserve requirement to 11.5 percent from 8.5 percent. It cut the reserve requirement to 9.5 percent two weeks ago. -- Jan Lopatka, Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
